items.title: 68533_Sam Jones oral history interview
items.q: George Russell, who we both know very well

ctx.x: So do you--I'm not trying to lead you but I'm just trying to sort of put it into uh, a certain kind of thing of what I think I hear you say in terms of--you know, and it's still trying to tie it back to the whole thing of defining what is jazz. One of the things that you said, you mentioned about repetition and how they don't seem to have no imagination, you just keep repeating the same thing over and over again and how it doesn't seem to have any imagination--and you say why can't you come up with something…

a part of the early Sixties and then things started turning around to a more of a group kind of thing where it's, like you say, more a mass appeal kind of sound and concept? You know, like, OK, I'll tell you where I'm coming from. George Russell, who we both know very well, you know, as done a lot as far as trying to come up with like a lot of theoretical concepts about getting jazz musicians to become more sophisticated, harmony with "Cubano Bee, Cubano Bop" with Dizzy.... and stuff like that./..George Russell…

fluence cause trying to figure out what has caused these different intracies. It seems like there is a lot of confusion going on with a lot of people. Like you said, the program directors, the people up there who are programming what they say is jazz and they don't, in your estimation and in mine also, they ain't playing no jazz. But do you think this is possibly some of it; have an influence, this idea of group orientation as opposed to individuals.
